# Evaluation bugs in the starter (generated by `python -m src.evaluate`)

All numbers come from `src/evaluate.py` on dev (n=4000, silver labels) with the unmodified starter
(`baseline/baseline.py`, threshold 0.1). Tables: `results/baseline_fixed.csv`; labelled confusion matrix: `results/baseline_confusion.csv`.

| # | Bug | Evidence | Effect |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Per-class rows attributed to the wrong class | `baseline/eval.py` passes `target_names` in taxonomy order, but sklearn sorts labels alphabetically. The row shown as `order_status` (support 212) really belongs to `account_help`. Column `starter_row_really_belongs_to` in baseline_fixed.csv gives the real class of every shown row. | Every per-class number in `baseline_dev.json` describes a different class than its name |
| 2 | "macro_f1" is weighted F1 | `f1_score(average="weighted")`, `baseline/eval.py:36` | Reported 0.446; weighted recomputed 0.446; true macro-F1 **0.411** |
| 3 | Confusion matrix saved without `labels=` | `confusion_matrix(y, pred)`: sorted-label order, no names | Unreadable as saved; now `results/baseline_confusion.csv` with names |
| 4 | Two intents can never be predicted | `promo_code_issue`, `account_help` have no taxonomy examples -> zero centroids. Classes with recall exactly 0 in the fixed report: promo_code_issue, account_help | 419 dev rows (10.5%) can never be correct |
| 4b | The starter's zero-recall rows were the wrong classes | Starter printed 0.00 recall for the rows named `order_status` and `change_address`, which really belong to `account_help` and `promo_code_issue` | Looked like two healthy-class failures while the real ones were invisible |
| 5 | Threshold 0.1 floods `out_of_scope` | 2161 of 4000 dev rows predicted `out_of_scope` (54.0%); true `out_of_scope` rows: 378 | `out_of_scope` precision 0.16, recall 0.91 |
| 7 | Data contains taxonomy examples verbatim | rows containing a normalised taxonomy example: train 7867/30000, dev 1001/4000, test 746/3000 (counts only, no test labels used) | Matching scores on those rows overstate generalisation; see slice rows in baseline_fixed.csv |
| 8 | Vectoriser vocabulary/IDF fitted on train **and dev** | `baseline/baseline.py:36`. Refit on train + taxonomy only: accuracy 0.4233 -> 0.4303, macro-F1 0.4105 -> 0.4152 | Size of the dev leak on the starter (unsupervised, so expected to be small) |
| 9 | Top-3 / MRR ignore the threshold | Starter ranks raw scores. With out_of_scope ranked first when best < 0.1: top-3 0.7200 -> 0.7208, MRR 0.6655 -> 0.5996 | Ranking metrics now describe the deployed system |
| 10 | Train/dev class shift | `promo_code_issue` train 1.1% vs dev 5.2%; `account_help` train 1.3% vs dev 5.3% | Matters from Phase 4 (training) |

Note on bug 4: both intents have all-zero centroids, so their cosine is always 0 and they never win the argmax against a positive score. Fixed recall is exactly 0 for them (rows in baseline_fixed.csv). The starter's report hid this: it showed 0.00 under the names `order_status` and `change_address` instead.

Bug 6 (taxonomy contradictions) and 11 (silver labels breaking the rules) are handled in Phases 2-3. Same example text under two different intents in `taxonomy.json`: ["'where's my food' in order_status and delivery_delay", "'my order is incomplete' in missing_item and wrong_item"].

## Reproduced vs shipped
Shipped `results/baseline_dev.json` has top-3 0.7192 / MRR 0.6652; the raw-score recompute here gives 0.7200 / 0.6655. The gap (<0.001) is unexplained; probably tie-breaking among tied scores across platforms (not investigated).

## Slice heuristics and their limits
- length: words after `clean()`; short <=6, medium 7-14, long >=15.
- Hinglish: message contains any token from a hand-written list of unambiguous Hindi words (`HINGLISH` in `src/evaluate.py`). Misses Hinglish made only of rare words; not validated against human labels.
- multi-request: regex for connectors ("also", "and", "but", "aur", "then", "actually"...). "and" also joins non-requests, so this over-counts.
- contains-taxonomy-example: normalised taxonomy example is a substring of the normalised message.
